content.text: Chapter Eleven
The First Blood Knights
For six days, Silvermoon tried to teach stone how to carry salvation.

The first wardstone held M’uru’s radiance for eleven minutes. The second cracked along an old flaw and filled the testing chamber with a warm gold mist that soothed everyone’s hunger until the magisters vented it into the vault. A third remained bright through the night, then surrendered all its stored power when an orderly touched it with an ungloved hand.

Healing foci fared better. One closed a laborer’s burned palm before its internal lattice spoiled. Another sent a pulse through two floors of the lower complex and briefly relieved every blood elf standing above it, including three guards who had not been told what the experiment was meant to do. By the time the result reached the nearest infirmary, the power had thinned into little more than warmth.

Falanaras spent those days carrying reports between the vault, the barracks, and Rommath’s clerks. It was work suited to a captain trusted with the secret and useless to anyone who wanted sleep. Each morning the maps showed new red routes into the city. Each evening half of them had been crossed out.
The seventh attempt reached farther than the rest.

Astalor had joined three silver conduits around a receiving vessel the size of a wine cask. From there, a buried line ran beneath Farstriders’ Square toward a small clinic serving reconstruction crews and the families housed near the eastern wall. Forty-three people waited inside under the pretense of a ward inspection. Two healers stood ready with ledgers and no explanation for their patients.
Falanaras watched from the upper gallery as the magisters opened the draw.

M’uru brightened inside the cage. Crimson force-chains tightened around its drifting sigils, and the chamber filled with the high, fractured cry Falanaras had first heard in Netherstorm. Light poured into the receiving vessel. The cask shuddered against its braces. Along the wall, crystal indicators woke in sequence—one, two, three, then all the way to the clinic relay.
A cheer rose from the western station.
It ended when the fourth indicator burst.

The conduit screamed beneath the floor. A seam of red-gold light raced back toward the vault, scorching mortar black as it came. Selorien threw both hands over the western relay and twisted the flow into an empty wardstone. Astalor severed the main channel an instant later. The vessel split down its middle and spilled radiance across the tiles.

Falanaras felt the ache behind his ribs vanish. Around him, magisters stopped with mouths open and hands slack. The relief lasted three breaths. Then the loose Light fled into the walls, and hunger returned with the intimate cruelty of a door shutting in one’s face.
Below, M’uru dimmed and recovered. Astalor closed every remaining control, then crossed to Selorien and examined his burned hand before looking to the split vessel and the gauges.
“Begin with the clinic,” Astalor said.
“The clinic received enough to ease twelve patients,” Selorien said. “Three reported nausea. One lost consciousness for several seconds. No lasting harm yet.”
“And the conduit?”
“Ruined.” Selorien opened his burned hand and regarded it without drama. “As is the receiving vessel.”

Rommath descended from the gallery. His robes passed through the fading radiance without stirring it. Lor’themar followed at a slower pace, his good eye moving over the split cask, the scorched wall, and the captive at the chamber’s center.
“Can it be corrected?” the regent asked.

Astalor crouched to examine a fragment of silver casing. “Yes, in time. The current resists interruption, divides poorly, and degrades outside a living vessel. Each failure has shown us another condition we must master. None lies beyond sin’dorei ability.”
“How long?”
“Longer than those waiting at the ration halls can afford,” Astalor said. “We should not confine our work to storage while they wait.”
Lor’themar’s expression hardened. “They have waited through every promise we have made them. Continue.”

“Of course. We will correct the distribution system.” Astalor glanced toward Liadrin. She had stood beside M’uru throughout the failed draw, close enough for its radiance to sharpen the edges of her armor. “In parallel, we have devised a method that already succeeds.”
Liadrin met his gaze. “For moments.”

“Our first design mistook the recipient for another vessel,” Astalor said. He indicated the broken cask without disdain, as though it had served its purpose by failing. “Stored power fades. Conduits leak. A living recipient can remain joined to the source.”
Falanaras remembered the Light fading from his hand before they reached Silvermoon. “You mean to bind the recipient directly to M’uru.”

A slight smile touched Astalor’s face. “A governed bond, replenishing because it remains joined to M’uru and narrow enough to preserve both source and recipient. We have already proved transfer. The problem before us is subjugation: claiming the terms under which M’uru yields and the recipient receives.”
The word settled across the chamber with greater weight than the broken equipment.

Rommath turned toward the upper galleries, where clerks and junior magisters watched from behind the rail. “You have all heard gentler names for what keeps this city alive. Rationing. Adaptation. Necessary practice. Those names have their uses. They do not alter the act.”
No one moved. Even the ward-crystals seemed quieter around his voice.

“Quel’Thalas does not owe the world a beautiful extinction,” Rommath said. “We will build the public channels. We will fill infirmaries and ration halls if it takes every magister in Silvermoon. While that work continues, we will use the method that succeeds. Survival first. Structure second. Interpretation after.”
Lor’themar studied M’uru. “And who risks this bond first?”
Liadrin stepped forward before Astalor could answer. “I do.”

Astalor rebuilt the receiving apparatus with the patient absorption of a scholar refining difficult work. He thanked orderlies who anticipated his needs and never softened the purpose: the new design would bind a living soul directly to a captive source. Falanaras found no malice in him. Astalor regarded every difficulty in governing M’uru’s power as another property to master and the binding as an achievement of sin’dorei ability.

He set four pylons around M’uru’s cage and joined them to a silver platform outside the inner restraint circle. Each pylon carried two controls: one governing the draw from M’uru, the other limiting what could reach the recipient. Selorien verified those limits independently and added a fifth line from the platform back into the cage. It would return excess current before it burned through the recipient or destabilized M’uru. Astalor approved it as the safeguard that made a sustained bond possible.

They worked through the night. By morning, a dozen soldiers and former temple guards waited in the gallery. Falanaras stood among them with Theron, Daric, and Captain Althene Starwind. None had been promised a place. They had been ordered to observe the first direct binding and decide afterward whether they wished to submit themselves for testing.
Lethira watched from farther back, arms folded over her ranger leathers. Her presence had required three signatures and an argument with a vault officer. She had acquired all four.

Liadrin entered wearing plain crimson plate, stripped of insignia. She carried no priest’s staff and offered no prayer. When she stepped onto the platform, M’uru’s sigils turned toward her with the slow attention of something that had been waiting.

Falanaras remembered her at Silvermoon’s inner gate, white and blue vestments stained with blood, calling on the Light as wounded civilians screamed around her. That woman had believed service made the power holy. The woman below had survived the answer to that belief.
Rommath took position beside the northern pylon. Astalor stood at the controls. Selorien remained near Liadrin with one hand hovering over the emergency severance rune.

“The bond may resist severance once it forms,” Astalor said. “You should expect pain, disorientation, and some loss of voluntary control. We have limited the initial draw to what your prior use of the Light suggests you can sustain. If you lose speech, raise your left hand. If you cannot raise it, Magister Dawnmark will sever the draw when your responses cross the limits we have set. We will not wait for collapse.”
“If he ends it too early?” Liadrin asked.
“Then the bond may fail, and we begin again after you recover. There is no useful result in losing you before we understand the method.”
“Then he will wait for my signal.”
Selorien checked the emergency severance rune. “I will wait while the readings permit it.”
Astalor opened the first control.

The force-chains pulled inward. M’uru’s song broke across the chamber, a bright harmony crushed into shrieking fragments. Light struck the pylons and became four narrow streams. They met above Liadrin, circled once, and descended through her armor without touching the metal.

Her back arched. Both hands closed into fists. Radiance spilled between the plates at her throat and wrists, too fierce to look at directly. The platform’s runes flared white, then red-gold as the restraint current bled into the transfer.

Falanaras knew the relief inside that agony. His brief test in Netherstorm had cleared the hunger so completely that its absence had frightened him. Liadrin received many times that measure now. Her face held the stillness of someone enduring a blade without granting it the satisfaction of movement.
“The bond remains within the limits we established,” Astalor said. “Increase the draw by one division.”
Selorien looked at Liadrin. She gave the smallest nod.

The second surge drove her to one knee. A sound escaped her then, low and furious. M’uru answered with another glass-edged cry. For one terrible instant Falanaras could not tell whether the pain in the chamber belonged to captive or recipient. The apparatus had joined them closely enough that the distinction ceased to offer comfort.
Liadrin raised her head.

Golden fire gathered around her empty hand. It tightened at her command, becoming a dense sphere no larger than an apple. She turned her wrist. The sphere unfolded into a radiant shield, held for three breaths, then collapsed into sparks that vanished before reaching the floor.
Astalor watched the gauges, pleasure warming his expression. “Excellent. The power is answering her intention rather than the pylons.”
“Stop the draw,” Lor’themar said from the shadow beneath the gallery.

Falanaras had not seen him enter. The regent stood without escort or ceremonial dress, one hand resting on the pommel of his sword. He had chosen the darkest part of the chamber and still refused the protection of absence.
Liadrin lifted her left hand. “Continue.”
“You have proved the transfer,” Lor’themar said.
“I have proved I can survive it. Those are different results.” Liadrin forced herself upright. “If others are to accept this bond, I will know the full weight first.”
Lor’themar’s jaw tightened. He did not countermand her.

The binding continued until sweat ran beneath Liadrin’s gorget and blood marked one nostril. Astalor guided the draw through several measured changes, announcing what he meant to test and waiting for Selorien’s confirmation before each one. At last he closed the source while the platform still held steady. M’uru’s song softened. Liadrin remained standing.
When the apparatus fell silent, the radiance around her did not disappear.

It diminished to a red-gold seam beneath her skin, visible at the eyes and along the hand she opened toward M’uru. The Light answered. A small flame rose above her palm and held there, fed through a channel no instrument now touched.
Astalor studied the gauges. The readings drew a slight smile from him. “Stable. The bond remains without the apparatus, and M’uru’s baseline has recovered. Magnificent.”
Selorien wrapped his burned hand around the edge of the console. “Stable, with measurable strain to source and recipient.”
“As expected,” Astalor replied. “We have made a single governed system of them. Our work now is to keep that strain survivable and the bond obedient.”
Liadrin extinguished the flame and faced the gallery. Fatigue had hollowed her cheeks, yet her voice carried to every waiting candidate.

“The Light did not save us,” she said. “It did not keep Arthas from our gates. It did not preserve the Sunwell, our children, or the dead we still speak to when sleep is poor. I served it faithfully, and faith did not make our suffering meaningful.”
Her gaze moved across soldiers, rangers, former temple guards, and Falanaras.

“If the Light will not save Quel’Thalas by grace, the sin’dorei will take from it what is needed and save ourselves. Do not mistake that declaration for innocence. M’uru suffers beneath us. Our enemies will call us profane, and some among our own people will agree. Remember the source. Remember the purpose. Then decide whether you can serve under both truths.”
She stepped down from the platform. No one cheered.
Daric was the first to descend from the gallery.
“Where do I stand?” he asked.
The trials lasted nine days.

Twenty-one candidates entered the lower complex. Seven failed the first attempt. Two lost consciousness before a direct binding could be established. One former priest broke into sobbing when M’uru’s voice entered his mind and could not be persuaded to return. Astalor recorded each failure in an orderly hand, separating rejection, physical shock, and loss of control as different problems. Three soldiers accepted the power easily, then kept drawing after Liadrin ordered them to release the source. Astalor began outlining stronger governor restraints. Liadrin dismissed them before he finished; a knight who required the apparatus to enforce obedience had already failed her test.

“Capacity without obedience is another form of weakness,” she told the remaining candidates. “You know this from taking power out of living currents. The Light does not excuse appetite. It gives appetite a sharper weapon.”

Daric endured his transfer with clenched teeth and a stare fixed on the cage. When the bond settled, he drew a practice sword and bound radiance along its edge. The stored Light released through his first strike in a compact burst that cracked a shield and nearly knocked its bearer into the wall. Liadrin made him repeat the exercise until he could choose how much of the bound force left the weapon. On the final attempt the shield moved one pace, the soldier behind it remained unbruised, and no radiance lingered on the blade after purpose ended.

Althene approached the Light as she approached a narrow trail: testing each step, wasting nothing. Her first healing attempt sealed a cut on Selorien’s forearm in a quick pulse so precisely that Astalor examined the sealed flesh, then asked whether she had served in a temple. She told him rangers learned to keep people alive where temples were unavailable. He accepted the correction with a slight nod. Liadrin then gave Althene a harder injury: a practice burn laced with a harmless arcane irritant that kept the skin inflamed. Althene learned to send the Light through the wound without closing it first. The foreign current came out as blue smoke. Only then did she seal the flesh.

Theron’s bond resisted for almost a minute. He stood inside the receiving circle with his shield planted before him, sweat darkening his collar as the stolen radiance broke around his armor. Liadrin watched from the circle’s edge and ordered him to hold. Then the current found him. A low, steady gold spread from his stance into the three candidates nearest him. Their shoulders settled. Their footing firmed. When the magisters sent practice bolts toward the group, Theron raised his shield and the same sustained current folded forward into a curved wall from its rim. Three impacts broke against it. The quieter strength around his companions remained until he dismissed it.
When it ended, he looked at Liadrin and said, “Useful.”
She almost smiled. “A ringing endorsement.”
Liadrin inclined her head toward the practice floor. “Set the shield down. The next test is harder.”

A candidate named Caerith lay on a cot beside the practice floor. The bond had rejected him that morning, leaving burns across his chest where the transfer current had sought paths his body could not hold. He was conscious, though each breath caught before completion. Two healers had salved the burns and steadied his heart. The remaining damage lay too deep for their exhausted reserves.
Theron crouched beside him. “You want me to heal this?”
“I want you to find out whether you can,” Liadrin said. “A wall is useful until someone falls behind it.”

Theron removed one gauntlet and placed his palm over Caerith’s sternum. His first attempt produced a flash that made the injured elf flinch. Theron withdrew at once. A shallow wound could have closed under that brief force; the damage beneath Caerith’s burns lay around lungs, heart, and exhausted muscle. Theron called a slower current and held it. The Light gathered around his fingers in an uneven glow, entered the burns, and spread deeper with each breath. Caerith’s next breath reached the bottom of his lungs. The one after it came without a catch.

M’uru cried below the working. Theron’s shoulders stiffened. He kept his hand in place until the healer touched his wrist and said the heart had steadied, then severed the call immediately. The glow died. Caerith slept.
“Still useful?” Falanaras asked when Theron joined him along the gallery rail.
Theron watched the healers carry Caerith toward recovery. “More than I wanted it to be.”

Beyond the dividing wall, the public-distribution team opened another receiving vessel. Its indicators rose, held, and failed one by one. Selorien crossed between the two experiments with a complete comparison for Astalor: the living bonds retained nearly all the power they received, while the latest storage crystal had lost two-thirds of its charge in under an hour. Astalor listened without interruption, then sent him back with revised safeguards for both teams. Rommath ordered both lines of work to continue.

The disparity changed the candidates’ posture. They had arrived expecting to become soldiers with an unfamiliar weapon. By the third evening, healers from two clinics had begun observing the trials. Astalor described trained recipients carrying stable charges to places the conduits could not yet reach, dwelling on the negligible loss. He called it an interim use of a method the sin’dorei had already mastered. No one called it an answer for the city. It was a bridge built from living bodies while the safer work lagged behind.
Theron flexed his bare hand. “Rynel would have hated the ceremony.”
“He would have corrected everyone’s stance during it.”

“And used the power.” Theron looked down at the faint radiance answering beneath his skin. “If someone had put it in his hands before Deatholme, he might have lived. If we put it in ours now, someone else might.”
It was the closest Theron came to explaining his choice. Falanaras understood. Theron had always built conviction from the person immediately behind his shield.

Falanaras went last on the fourth day. Astalor explained that the earlier exposure had given the Light a familiar path and improved the chance of a stable bond, though it removed neither pain nor risk. Falanaras believed him. The restraints made belief no comfort.

Liadrin faced him inside the circle. Her bond had altered her in small ways. Her eyes held a gold ember beneath their fel-green glow, and fine tremors sometimes passed through her fingers after a heavy draw. She hid neither.
“You remember the first test,” she said.
“Every moment.”
“That will work against you. You will anticipate relief and pull toward it. Do not reach. Receive.”
After Astalor and Selorien independently confirmed every safeguard, the apparatus opened a channel from M’uru toward him.

M’uru’s pain came first. The cry entered Falanaras behind the eyes, immense and intimate. Then the Light followed along the channel. It drove through muscle, scar, and memory, finding every absence the Sunwell had left in him. Hunger vanished. Grief remained. For a heartbeat he mistook the distinction for mercy.

He wanted to seize the current and make abundance itself the proof. Rynel at the ward-anchor returned to him. The captain had spent every measure the escape required, then turned the strength away from his own hunger and toward the soldiers depending on him. He had chosen what power was for.
Falanaras opened his hand instead of closing it.

The current settled. A bond remained behind it, narrow and bright, running directly toward the captive presence at the city’s heart. He could feel the Light waiting there. It no longer filled him without end. It answered when he called, and every answer carried the faint echo of broken music.
“Now give it purpose,” Liadrin said.

A practice target stood at the far edge of the chamber, armored in layered wards meant to imitate Scourge resistance. Falanaras drew his glaive. The Light was not hostile magic to drain, but his spellbreaker training still showed him where the target’s protections crossed and which layer governed the rest. He bound red-gold radiance along the crescent blade and gave the stored force a point of release: the weakest crossing, on contact, and nowhere else.

The first strike released only enough holy force to rupture the governing ward. The remaining protections dimmed with it. Falanaras rebound the Light along the blade, stepped through the opening, and discharged the second store into the target’s armored center. Red-gold fire crossed from shoulder to hip and left the cut edges smoking. The glaive went dark the instant the work was complete.

Astalor looked from the ruined target to his gauges. “Excellent. You broke the governing ward, held the second charge until contact, and ended the call when its purpose was complete. The bond answered your intention exactly.”
“You called Lady Liadrin’s result excellent,” Selorien said.
“It was accurate then as well.”

Later, while healers checked the burning behind Falanaras’s eyes, Liadrin sat beside him on the lowest gallery step. The chamber had emptied except for guards and the tireless magisters working on another public-distribution vessel beyond the wall.
“You governed it,” she said.
“Rynel taught me the lesson late.”

“Late lessons still count.” She flexed one trembling hand. “You accepted enough to destroy the target and put it where it belonged. That is discipline. You are trying to decide whether accepting the power makes you responsible for every cry below us.”
“Doesn’t it?”

“Yes.” Liadrin gave him no pause in which to hope for comfort. “It also makes you responsible for what you do with the power. Refusing one burden does not remove the other. It only chooses which lives receive your loyalty.”
“You make it sound simple.”

“It is unbearable. That is different.” Her gaze shifted toward M’uru. “If you join what we are building, do not offer half an oath. Do not serve while imagining your private reluctance keeps your hands untouched. Know exactly what we are, and remain in service anyway.”

Falanaras looked through the bars of the restraint field. M’uru’s sigils drifted in their patient revolutions. The naaru had entered Astalor’s cage willingly in Tempest Keep. It remained now beneath a city that had learned to call captivity a system.
“I will decide before the oath,” he said.
Liadrin rose. “See that you do.”
They told Lethira on the western terrace where she had welcomed Falanaras home.

The city below had grown accustomed to new rumors. Citizens spoke of a sealed reliquary under Farstriders’ Square, a weapon from Outland, a restored fragment of the Sunwell, or a private source reserved for the ruling houses. The official notices mentioned improved ward research and asked for patience at ration stations.
Lethira sat on the parapet with one boot braced against the stone. “You both have the expression people wear before volunteering for something unpleasant.”
Theron leaned his shield against the wall. A faint gold line remained around its rim from the morning’s exercises. “We are joining Liadrin’s order.”
“It has an order now?”
“By tomorrow,” Falanaras said.
Lethira’s eyes moved between them. “What does it require?”
Theron answered first. “Discipline. Training. A willingness to be hated by anyone who learns where the power comes from.”
“So military service with brighter uniforms.”
Theron considered. “The uniforms are darker.”
She looked at Falanaras. The humor eased from her face. “And you?”

“I have spent years learning to take hostile magic and decide what it becomes in my hands. This is harder because the source is innocent.” He rested both palms on the terrace rail. “It works. I can protect people with it. I can kill the things that still cross the Dead Scar. I cannot make M’uru’s captivity righteous.”
“That was almost recognizable,” Lethira said quietly.
“I intend to become one of them.”
She nodded once, accepting the statement without blessing it. Then she tapped the bow at her shoulder.
“No thanks. I’ll stick to my bow.”
Theron lifted one eyebrow. “We had assumed.”
“Good. I would hate to think the Light had damaged your judgment.” Lethira stood and offered each of them a forearm. “Try not to become insufferable before your first deployment.”

Falanaras clasped her arm. The three of them remained on the terrace until the ward-lamps came alive below. Their paths had diverged before and would again. For that evening, the differences still fit inside the reach of their hands.
The founding took place beneath Farstriders’ Square before dawn.

Fourteen candidates remained. They wore black tabards edged in crimson over whatever armor had carried them through the trials. The cloth was new, the equipment beneath it scarred and mismatched. Daric stood near the front. Althene had tied her ranger’s braid back with a strip of black ribbon. Theron rested both hands on his shield. Falanaras carried his glaive upright beside him.

The magisters had opened the aperture above M’uru’s vault. Light rose through it in a broad red-gold column, colored by the restraints it passed. The candidates formed two lines around the opening. No altar stood between them and the captive. Liadrin had refused one.

Rommath and Astalor waited at the chamber’s edge. Selorien stood with the access ledger. Lor’themar occupied the same shadowed place from which he had witnessed Liadrin’s binding. He spoke to no one and claimed no ceremonial role. His presence denied every official above him the excuse of believing the decision belonged to lesser hands.

Liadrin entered in black and crimson plate. A new ranseur rested in her hand, its blade dark red along the edge. The Light moved beneath her skin in faint pulses synchronized with the radiance rising from below.
She took her place at the head of the aperture.

“The old orders were founded in devotion,” she said. “Their knights served the Light and trusted that service to answer them. We stand here because trust failed, because our kingdom burned, and because survival demanded power that would answer discipline.”
She lowered the ranseur until its point hovered above the column.

“We carry the blood of those Quel’Thalas lost and the blood we will spend in its defense. We wield a captive Light. We will neither disguise its source nor surrender its strength. From this hour, we are Blood Knights.”
The name entered the chamber without applause. Falanaras felt it settle onto him with the weight of armor issued before a battle.
Liadrin planted the ranseur’s butt against the floor. “Kneel.”
Fourteen candidates knelt around M’uru’s rising radiance.
“Whom do you serve?”
“Quel’Thalas,” they answered.
“What do you bear?”
“The strength our people require. The cost by which it came.”
“What governs your hand?”
“Discipline. Duty. Honor. Remembrance.”
Liadrin’s gaze moved down the line. “Spend what the task requires. Obey command. When purpose ends, so does force. Rise, Blood Knights.”

Falanaras stood beside Theron. The bond opened at the motion, and stolen Light entered him in a controlled current. It eased the hunger, strengthened the hand around his glaive, and carried M’uru’s distant cry through the chamber. Pride rose with it—fierce, unwelcome, and his own.

He had chosen this. The order would defend roads, close wounds, break the undead, and give soldiers strength no enemy expected from a people already dangerous to magic. Those truths deserved their full measure. So did the being held below them.
No absolution came. Falanaras had ceased waiting for it.

Above them, Silvermoon woke beneath crimson banners and ward-lamps, its clinics still waiting for conduits that could carry relief without failing. Below, M’uru remained in chains. Between city and captive stood the first Blood Knights, carrying power enough to save lives and knowledge enough to understand the wound beneath it.
